extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of drama/poetics; playwrights and writers studying tragic drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing and evaluating tragic drama, emphasizing the primacy of plot, the nature of the tragic hero, and the relations among plot, character (ἦθος), and thought/dianoia (διάνοια). Useful for writers, critics, and students analyzing tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal tragic hero
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle describes an ideal tragedy with an ideal hero to correspond: a figure who excites pity and fear in no ordinary combination, but these two emotions heightened to their utmost capacity under perfect art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hero should not be 'faultily faultless' nor a consummate villain; rather, a figure whose weakness and strength alike bring him within common humanity. Modern drama (e.g., Shakespeare) expands the meaning of the tragic ἁμαρτία: noble natures ruined through some defect of character. Examples: Hamlet, Othello, Lear, Macbeth, Coriolanus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of fortune (περιπέτεια / peripeteia)
rubrics_metrics.description: The change of fortune in ideal tragedy is often the specific kind called περιπέτεια — a sudden reversal of fortune brought about by the very means which seemed adapted to produce the contrary effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be a reversal that is causally linked to the action/means of the play (example: in Oedipus Tyrannus the expected means of proving innocence becomes the most convincing proof of guilt). Reversal is a decisive plot moment that powerfully awakens tragic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal tragedy 'will excite pity and fear'—the emotions are central to tragic effect and should be intensified by the play's artistic structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plot's inner structure (not mere rhetorical exhortation) is the medium by which pity and fear are conveyed. Lesser works may still be tragedies if they evoke these emotions to a lesser degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot (μῦθος) as primary element / 'soul' of tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot is the first principle and, as it were, the soul of the tragedy: the animating principle around which parts grow and group themselves; the origin of movement and the basis of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plot is an imitation of action (not merely external events) and gives the play its inner meaning and unity. To evaluate a tragic play, examine the coherence, intentionality, and teleology of its plot—the plot should realize the play's intention and contain decisive moments (reversals, recognitions) that produce the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action must be an organic, complete whole (beginning, middle, end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic action must form a complete whole: a coherent series of events standing in organic relation to one another and bound by the law of cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated deed, however terrible, is not enough; action must be developed and show motives, consequences, and reciprocal effects on characters. Look for causal necessity/probability and the plot's internal centre or pivot around which events turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict is essential and must have outward manifestation
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama implies conflict — collision of forces (external necessity, inward divided will, other human wills) — and this conflict is the soul of the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts that remain purely mental without outward acts are not properly dramatic. Even inward conflict must have an outward side: concrete acts or relations with the external world that tie it into the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character (ἦθος) defined and its role
rubrics_metrics.description: ἦθος is the moral element of character: an expression of moral purpose, permanent disposition and tendencies. In Aristotle's Poetics, ἦθος and διάνοια are two factors that constitute the person and are causes of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character is revealed through speeches and actions; but Aristotle stresses the subordination of ἦθος to plot—character derives dramatic value through its relation to action. Evaluate how well characters' moral dispositions produce and justify their actions within the plot's logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dianoia (διάνοια) — thought / intellectual element
rubrics_metrics.description: διάνοια is the intellectual element: the speaker's reasoning, proofs, disproofs, and general maxims; in drama it is typically manifested in speech and in the shaping idea behind incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dianoia may appear as dramatic λόγοι (speeches) or be embodied in the plot (the poet's thought). Assess how the play's ideas and reasoning are integrated into speeches and the action, and whether they serve dramatic rather than purely rhetorical ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic dialogue must serve action, not replace it
rubrics_metrics.description: In drama, persons converse to explain their doings and influence others; speeches should not be abstract mathematical truths but connected to motives and action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid ethical monologues or rhetorical displays that substitute talk for enacted plot. Such passages may be 'preliminaries of tragedy' but not the tragic action itself. Evaluate whether dialogue advances action and reveals character rather than merely stating maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be active / energetic (fit for drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic character has some vital and spontaneous force: it must be able to make and mould circumstances and express will in deed rather than being merely passive feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive, purely emotional characters are more suited to lyric poetry. Exceptions (e.g., Hamlet) show intellectual inactivity becoming a form of action; but generally assess whether the character's will produces decisive action that drives the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability / necessity governs speeches and actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The law of necessity or probability should prescribe not only the plot but also the speeches and actions of the dramatic persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions and speeches must be credible within the world of the play; assess if character motives and events follow convincing necessity or probability rather than arbitrary contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot should not be complicated for its own sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot need not be 'complicated' — complication is not an end in itself. Many great Greek tragedies are singularly simple in structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the unity and organic necessity of incidents rather than the density of twists. A tightly unified, causally integrated simple plot can be superior to unnecessary entanglement designed to excite curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action and character interrelation: action should spring from and reflect character
rubrics_metrics.description: Higher dramatic conditions are satisfied when action springs out of character and reflects it; tragic drama represents the destiny of the individual where inner and outer correspond closely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the protagonist's deeds are the logical outcome of their dispositional character (i.e., 'man's character is his destiny'), so the catastrophe appears as the character's own self-recoil rather than an external arbitrary fate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show, don't tell — characters must 'enact' their story
rubrics_metrics.description: In drama the characters are not described, they enact their own story and so reveal themselves; we know them by what we see them do rather than by narrated description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate dramatic effectiveness by how well characterization is achieved through enacted decisions and deeds rather than through descriptive exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of failing to adapt inherited material to new ethical ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: When dramatists work with traditional/legendary material, the fixed outlines of the myth may limit development of character and plot, and adaptation is required to reconcile old facts with new ethical sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the playwright successfully transforms inherited stories to fit contemporary dramatic and ethical aims, or whether the material yields inconsistency (as argued for Euripides).
